content: The primary diagnostic feature of a Type 2 reaction, also known as erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL), is the presence of inflamed nodules in the skin. These nodules, which are not associated with the skin lesions of leprosy, can appear anywhere on the body. They are located in the subcutaneous tissues and typically measure 1–2 cm in diameter. In severe cases, these nodules may ulcerate. Other clinical features that contribute to the severity of ENL include pain, fever, the number and extent of ENL lesions, peripheral edema, bone pain, joint or digit inflammation, lymphadenopathy, and nerve tenderness. An acute episode of ENL usually lasts between one and two weeks. ENL can be classified into three types: 1. Acute ENL: Episodes lasting less than six months, with treatment gradually withdrawn and no recurrence while on treatment. 2. Recurrent ENL: At least one additional episode occurring 28 days or more after treatment withdrawal. 3. Chronic ENL: Episodes lasting longer than six months, requiring continuous treatment or with treatment-free periods of less than 28 days. Patients with ENL often experience a reduced quality of life and significant economic burdens. They should be informed that ENL may persist for over a year or longer and counseled on symptom management. Patients should receive educational materials about steroids, including a steroid information leaflet and a Steroid Card, and be advised against purchasing over-the-counter steroids. Monitoring by a clinician experienced in managing ENL is essential. Depression related to the condition and its treatment should also be addressed during clinical visits. Laboratory investigations are not required to confirm ENL diagnosis but are necessary to monitor complications from immunosuppressant drugs. Regular nerve function assessments are also indicated. Treated leprosy patients may experience neuropathic pain, such as tingling or burning sensations in treated skin lesions, hands, or feet. This pain can be misdiagnosed as a reaction. In the absence of nerve tenderness or new nerve function impairment (NFI), neuropathic pain should be considered, especially if the original leprosy diagnosis was made more than 3–5 years earlier. Treatment should follow an analgesic ladder, starting with paracetamol, then non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., ibuprofen), and, if necessary, amitriptyline. Gabapentin may be used for refractory pain. Steroids are not recommended for neuropathic pain in leprosy. Disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) measure the overall disease burden, combining years lived with disability and years of life lost due to ill health or premature death. Leprosy-related mortality can result from ENL, steroid use, dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome, or suicide. DALYs do not adequately capture mental health issues, stigma, or the disabling effects of plantar ulceration. Studies show that, on average, 30% of a leprosy-affected person’s working life is lost due to disability. Nerve function assessment is critical for managing leprosy reactions and neuritis. All programs and clinics treating leprosy should increase routine nerve function testing using tools like ballpoint pens or nylon monofilaments. Testing should be precise and well-documented to monitor changes over time. Untreated NFI within six months of onset can lead to irreversible nerve damage and permanent disability. The goals of nerve function assessment include diagnosing leprosy, detecting NFI during or after treatment, monitoring changes in nerve function, and reducing stigma and discrimination. Sensory testing involves evaluating light touch using a ballpoint pen, a single monofilament, or a set of graded monofilaments. Testing is typically limited to the palms and soles, with 4–10 sites tested on each hand or foot. Proper demonstration and patient understanding are essential. Results should be documented to track changes over time. Ballpoint pens are widely available and can be effective if used carefully, but nylon monofilaments provide more standardized and accurate results. A 10-gram monofilament is preferred for detecting established neuropathy, while a 2-gram monofilament may indicate earlier NFI. Graded monofilaments, ranging from 70 mg to 300 gm, can detect varying levels of sensory loss but require a quiet environment and significant time for testing. Voluntary muscle testing (VMT) assesses the strength of specific muscles against resistance. Two scales are commonly used: a simpler three-category scale (Strong, Weak, Paralyzed) and the more detailed six-category Medical Research Council (MRC) Scale. Regular testing and documentation are crucial to identify changes in muscle strength.
